  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the brim of his hat.

He sat in the last pew until the woman who cleaned the church came with her bucket. She asked whether someone had died. He moved his knees to let her pass.

Outside, the gulls were back. He heard them quarrelling over something behind the fish shed. The tide was where the tide should have been.

He took the road to Maren's house.

All eleven posts stood straight. Her lantern lay beside the third, its glass unbroken. Tobias picked it up by the handle and carried it without letting it strike his leg.

The front door was shut.

He knocked once, then tried the latch. It lifted easily. In the front room the lamp stood on the sill, unlit. There was the chip in its base. There was her father's rug.

He set the lantern by the door. He had come prepared to call her name, but inside the house it seemed a thing he ought to have asked permission to do.

On the kitchen table lay half a loaf beneath a cloth. He touched the cut end. It had hardened overnight.

Before leaving, he returned to the front room and moved the lamp from the sill to the table beside her chair.

From there it could not be seen from the beach.

He closed the door carefully. Then he stood with his thumb against the latch, unable to remember whether he had found it open.",

  "text": "For three days Tobias took the upper road, though it added half a mile to his walk.

On the fourth, the baker asked whether Maren still wanted her Thursday loaf. Tobias said he would find out. The baker wrapped it before he could say anything else.

He carried it beneath his coat. Rain had begun, too fine to hear against the roofs.

At her gate he counted the posts without meaning to. Eleven. A strand of bladderwrack hung from the lowest wire, beyond the reach of any ordinary tide. He unhooked it and laid it on the ground.

This time he knocked twice.

The house smelled of cold ashes. Her lantern remained beside the door, and the lamp was where he had put it. He stood a moment looking at the empty sill.

In the kitchen, the old loaf lay beneath its cloth. A little blue mould had appeared along the crust. He took it outside for the birds, then put the fresh loaf in its place.

He looked through the cupboards for a plate. There were four, stacked with folded paper between them. He chose the top one and set the bread on it.

Before he left, he filled the kettle. The pump caught on the first stroke and yielded on the second, striking the bottom with a noise that made him turn.

Nothing had changed in the front room.

On his way home he stopped at the baker's and paid.

“Next Thursday?” the baker asked.

Tobias brushed a wet crumb from his sleeve.

“For now,” he said.",
